Ch 6.3 — Pipe Flow Losses III: Minor Losses

Fittings, valves, bends, entrances & exits · the loss coefficient K · complete pipe-system energy balance · text §6.7

Lectures 6.1 and 6.2 dealt with friction along straight pipe runs — the major loss \(h_f\), found from Darcy–Weisbach with a friction factor read off the Moody chart. But no real piping system is just a long straight tube. Between the reservoirs sit an entrance, a pump, elbows, tees, valves, bends, area changes, and an exit. Every one of these disturbs the flow locally — the streamlines separate, swirl, and re-attach — and that disorder dissipates mechanical energy. These localized losses are called minor losses, \(h_m\). This lecture shows how to quantify each one with a single dimensionless number, the loss coefficient \(K\), and then assemble every major and minor loss into one energy balance for the whole system.

Where Are the Losses in a Real System?

It helps to picture the whole circuit at once. Water is lifted from a lower reservoir to a higher one by a pump. Energy is lost at many points and added at one (the pump):

Figure 6.3.1 — A pump-and-pipe circuit between two reservoirs. Major losses occur along the straight suction and discharge lines; minor losses occur at every local connection (entrance, tee, gradual contraction, valve, elbows, bend, exit). The pump adds head. (White & Xue, Fig. 6.18 style.)
Major vs Minor Losses

Major losses \(h_f\) are the distributed friction losses along the straight pipe runs — the “along the pipe” losses of §6.1, set by \(f\), \(L/d\) and the velocity head.

Minor losses \(h_m\) are the localized losses at every fitting where the flow is disturbed: pipe entrance and exit, sudden or gradual area change, bends, elbows, tees, and valves.

A pump (or turbine) is neither — it adds (or removes) head and enters the energy equation with its own term.

“Minor” describes the location, not the size
Minor losses are not necessarily small. The head lost across a nearly-closed valve can exceed the friction loss of a long pipe. The word “minor” only means the loss is local (concentrated at a fitting) rather than distributed along the pipe. On short, fitting-heavy systems the minor losses often dominate.

The Complete Head-Loss Picture

Recall the head form of the energy equation from §5.4 (Eq. Sheet #43), written between two points 1 and 2 of a system that may contain a pump and/or a turbine:

Energy Equation with Losses & Machines
\[ \left(\frac{p_1}{\gamma}+\frac{V_1^2}{2g}+z_1\right) = \left(\frac{p_2}{\gamma}+\frac{V_2^2}{2g}+z_2\right) + h_{\text{loss}} - h_{\text{pump}} + h_{\text{turbine}} \]

Every term is a head (a length, in metres or feet of fluid). The total head loss bundles all the friction in the system — both the straight-pipe (major) losses and the fitting (minor) losses:

\[ h_{\text{loss}} = \sum h_f + \sum h_m \]
\(p/\gamma\) — pressure head (m) \(V^2/2g\) — velocity head (m) \(z\) — elevation head (m) \(h_{\text{loss}}\) — total head loss, always ≥ 0 (m) \(\sum h_f\) — sum of major (pipe-friction) losses (m) \(\sum h_m\) — sum of minor (fitting) losses (m) \(h_{\text{pump}}\) — head ADDED by a pump (m) \(h_{\text{turbine}}\) — head REMOVED by a turbine (m)

The sign pattern is the part students forget: + loss, − pump, + turbine. A pump adds energy so it appears on the far side with a minus sign (it reduces what the inlet has to supply); a turbine and all losses remove energy so they carry plus signs. Everything in this lecture goes into the \(\sum h_m\) bucket.

The Minor-Loss Coefficient K

The flow pattern through a fitting is far too complicated to predict from first principles, so minor losses are measured experimentally and reported as a multiple of the velocity head \(V^2/2g\) of the pipe the fitting sits in:

Minor Loss — Loss Coefficient Form
\[ h_m = K\,\frac{V^2}{2g} \qquad\text{and equivalently}\qquad h_m = \frac{\Delta p}{\rho g} \]

The dimensionless loss coefficient \(K\) packages all the messy geometry of one fitting into a single number. Multiply it by the velocity head to get the head lost; multiply by \(\rho g\) (i.e. \(\gamma\)) to get the local pressure drop.

\(h_m\) — minor (local) head loss (m) \(K\) — loss coefficient (dimensionless) \(V\) — average velocity in the pipe (m/s) \(g\) — gravitational acceleration (9.81 m/s²) \(\Delta p\) — local pressure drop across the fitting (Pa) \(\rho\) — fluid density (kg/m³)
★ Tip — read the velocity head from the right pipe
\(K\) is always tied to a particular velocity head. For most fittings that is just the pipe velocity. But for an area change (sudden or gradual contraction/expansion) the convention is to base \(h_m\) on the velocity head of the smaller pipe — the faster stream. Always confirm which \(V\) a chart or table assumes before you plug in.

One Pipe, Several Losses — The Combined Formula

If the pipe has a single, constant diameter then the velocity \(V\) is the same everywhere — in the straight runs, the fittings, and the valves. That lets us factor the common velocity head out of every term and add the losses in one shot:

Total Loss in a Single-Diameter Pipe
\[ h_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{\sum f\,\frac{L}{d}\,\frac{V^2}{2g}}_{\text{major losses}} + \underbrace{\sum K\,\frac{V^2}{2g}}_{\text{minor losses}} = \frac{V^2}{2g}\left(\frac{f}{d}\,\Sigma L + \Sigma K\right) \]

Sum every straight length into \(\Sigma L\) and every fitting coefficient into \(\Sigma K\), then apply one velocity head. This is the working form used in almost every single-pipe system problem.

\(h_{\text{total}}\) — total head loss in the pipe (m) \(f\) — Darcy friction factor (dimensionless) \(\Sigma L\) — sum of straight-pipe lengths (m) \(d\) — pipe diameter (m) \(\Sigma K\) — sum of all minor-loss coefficients \(V\) — common pipe velocity (m/s) \(g\) — gravitational acceleration (9.81 m/s²)
Multiple pipe sizes ⇒ compute each segment separately
The single-velocity factoring above only works because \(V\) is constant. As soon as the system has more than one diameter, the velocity head changes from segment to segment (continuity: \(V = Q/A\)). You must then evaluate the losses separately for each pipe size, each with its own \(V\), and only then add the head losses together.

Where Do the K Values Come From?

The rest of this lecture is a tour of the standard charts and tables that supply \(K\). You are not expected to memorize the numbers — you are expected to know which chart to read and how to read it. Keep these figures handy; they are the working reference for every minor-loss problem.

Valves

A valve’s loss depends on its type and, crucially, on how far it is open. The common types — gate, globe, angle, and check — have very different internal geometries and therefore very different losses even when fully open:

Figure 6.3.2 — The four common valve types in cutaway. A gate valve (left) gives a nearly straight-through path when open (low \(K\)); a globe valve (right) forces the flow through a tortuous S-path (high \(K\)); an angle valve turns the flow 90°; a check valve allows flow one way only.

For a partially open valve the loss coefficient climbs steeply as the valve closes — by one to three orders of magnitude. These curves give \(K\) versus the fraction open:

Figure 6.3.3 — Loss coefficient of partially open valves. Left: a butterfly valve, \(K\) vs opening angle (note the log scale — \(K\) ranges from <1 wide open to several hundred nearly shut). Right: gate, disk and globe valves, \(K\) vs fractional opening \(h/D\). The 55%-open gate valve in this lecture’s worked example is read from a curve like these.

Fittings — Elbows, Tees & Bends

Fitting losses depend on the type, the size, and the surface roughness. A long-radius elbow loses less than a sharp one; flow straight through the run of a tee loses less than flow turned into the branch:

Figure 6.3.4 — Standard threaded/flanged fittings. Gentler turns (long-radius elbows) and straight-through tee paths have the lowest \(K\); sharp turns and branch-flow tees have the highest.

The single most-used reference is the table of loss coefficients for typical valves and fittings, organized by nominal diameter and by connection style (screwed vs flanged):

Figure 6.3.5 — Loss coefficients \(K\) for typical fully-open valves and fittings (White & Xue, Table 6.5). Note two trends: \(K\) decreases as the pipe gets larger, and flanged fittings generally lose less than screwed ones. These are estimates — manufacturers’ tables should be used in practice.
★ Tip — reading the table
Match three things before you pull a number: the fitting type (row), the connection (Screwed or Flanged block), and the nominal diameter (column). Example: a 2-in screwed fully-open globe valve gives \(K = 6.9\); a 2-in screwed regular 90° elbow gives \(K = 0.95\). Both appear in this lecture’s worked example.

Pipe Entrance

Where the pipe draws fluid from a reservoir, the local loss depends on how rounded the entrance is. A sharp-edged inlet forces the flow to separate and contract (a vena contracta), losing roughly half a velocity head; rounding the lip dramatically cuts the loss:

Figure 6.3.6 — Entrance loss vs roundness. A sharp-edged inlet gives \(K \approx 0.5\); a filleted inlet falls along the curve. For a 10-in pipe with a \(r = 1\)-in fillet (\(r/d = 0.1\)), \(K \approx 0.12\).

Sudden Expansion & Contraction

An abrupt change in pipe diameter is a strong loss. The coefficient depends on the diameter ratio \(d/D\) (small to large), and — importantly — the velocity head is taken in the smaller pipe:

Figure 6.3.7 — Sudden expansion and sudden contraction, \(K\) vs \(d/D\), with \(h_m = K\,V^2/2g\) based on the smaller-pipe velocity. Example: a 6-in pipe suddenly connected to a 10-in pipe (\(d/D = 0.6\)) gives \(K \approx 0.4\).

Gradual Expansion & Contraction

Replacing the abrupt step with a gentle cone (a diffuser or nozzle) reduces the loss substantially. \(K\) now depends on both the diameter ratio and the cone angle — small cone angles keep the flow attached and the loss low:

Figure 6.3.8 — Gradual transitions. Left: gradual contraction, \(K\) vs \(d_1/d_2\). Right: gradual expansion (diffuser), \(K\) vs \(d_2/d_1\). Loss grows with cone angle; the loss is again based on the smaller-pipe velocity head.

Bends

A bend loss grows with the turn angle and shrinks as the bend is made more gradual (larger radius). It is plotted against the ratio \(R/d\) (bend radius to pipe diameter) for several bend angles:

Figure 6.3.9 — Bend loss, \(K\) vs \(R/d\), for 45°, 90° and 180° turns. The inset shows the secondary flow (a counter-rotating vortex pair) that the curvature induces. Surface roughness is not included. Example: a 1-in pipe bent 90° with \(R = 1\) ft (\(R/d = 12\)) gives \(K \approx 0.4\).
★ Tip — standard entrance/exit values worth remembering
Two values recur on nearly every reservoir-to-reservoir problem: a sharp entrance is \(K \approx 0.5\), and a sharp (submerged) exit is \(K = 1.0\). The exit is always \(1.0\) because the pipe’s entire kinetic energy \(V^2/2g\) is dumped and dissipated in the downstream reservoir — none is recovered.

Worked Example — Pump Horsepower for a Two-Reservoir System

This is the capstone problem of the chapter: a complete system with a pump, friction, and six minor losses. It ties together everything from §6.1–6.3.

Example — Pump Power Required

Water (\(\rho = 1.94\ \text{slug/ft}^3\), \(\nu = 0.000011\ \text{ft}^2/\text{s}\)) is pumped between two reservoirs at \(Q = 0.2\ \text{ft}^3/\text{s}\) through \(400\ \text{ft}\) of \(2\text{-in}\) diameter pipe with several minor losses, as shown. The roughness ratio is \(\varepsilon/d = 0.001\). Compute the pump horsepower required.

Example setup: \(z_1 = 20\) ft, \(z_2 = 120\) ft. Minor losses (in flow order): sharp entrance, open globe valve, pump, 12-in-radius bend, screwed regular 90° elbow, 55%-open gate valve, sharp exit.
▸ Show full solution

Thought process

The two reservoir surfaces are the natural points 1 and 2: both are open to atmosphere (gauge \(p = 0\)) and so wide that the surface velocities are essentially zero. That kills four of the six terms in the energy equation and leaves the elevation difference balanced against the losses and the pump.

This is a rating-style calculation (we know \(Q\), \(d\), \(L\), \(\varepsilon/d\)): march \(V \to \mathrm{Re}_d \to f\) for the major loss, look up each \(K\) for the minor losses, then solve the energy equation for \(h_{\text{pump}}\) and convert to power. Single constant diameter, so the combined single-velocity formula applies.

Given: \(\rho = 1.94\ \text{slug/ft}^3\), \(\nu = 1.1\times10^{-5}\ \text{ft}^2/\text{s}\), \(Q = 0.2\ \text{ft}^3/\text{s}\), \(L = 400\ \text{ft}\), \(d = \tfrac{2}{12}\ \text{ft}\), \(\varepsilon/d = 0.001\), \(z_1 = 20\ \text{ft}\), \(z_2 = 120\ \text{ft}\).  Find: pump power (hp).

Assumptions: steady incompressible flow; reservoir surfaces \(V_1 \approx V_2 \approx 0\); gauge pressures \(p_1 = p_2 = 0\); single constant-diameter pipe so \(V\) is common to all losses.

📋 Formulas Needed

1. Head equation \(\;\frac{p_1}{\gamma}+\frac{V_1^2}{2g}+z_1 = \frac{p_2}{\gamma}+\frac{V_2^2}{2g}+z_2 + h_f + \sum h_m - h_p\;\) — Eq. Sheet #43

2. Continuity / velocity \(\;V = Q/A,\ A=\tfrac{\pi}{4}d^2\;\) — Eq. Sheet #18

3. Reynolds number \(\;\mathrm{Re}_d = Vd/\nu\;\) — Eq. Sheet #47

4. Darcy–Weisbach + minor losses \(\;h_f+\sum h_m = \frac{V^2}{2g}\!\left(\frac{fL}{d}+\sum K\right)\;\) — Eq. Sheet #48, #57, #59

5. Pump power \(\;P = \rho g\,Q\,h_p\;\) — Eq. Sheet #45

1

Reduce the energy equation and solve for pump head

With \(p_1=p_2=0\) and \(V_1=V_2\approx0\), the head equation collapses to

\[ z_1 = z_2 + h_f + \sum h_m - h_p \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; h_p = (z_2-z_1) + h_f + \sum h_m \]

Using the combined single-diameter loss (constant \(V\)):

\[ h_p = (z_2 - z_1) + \frac{V^2}{2g}\left(\frac{fL}{d} + \sum K\right) = (120-20)\ \text{ft} + \frac{V^2}{2g}\left(\frac{fL}{d} + \sum K\right) \]

2

Find the velocity

\[ V = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{0.2\ \text{ft}^3/\text{s}}{\tfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\tfrac{2}{12}\ \text{ft}\right)^2} = \frac{0.2\ \text{ft}^3/\text{s}}{0.02182\ \text{ft}^2} = 9.17\ \text{ft/s} \]

3

Sum the minor-loss coefficients

Read each \(K\) from the lecture charts and tables (single 2-in screwed line):

Minor lossSource\(K\)
Sharp entranceFig. 6.3.60.5
Open globe valve (2-in, screwed)Table 6.56.9
12-in bend (\(R/d=\tfrac{12}{2}=6\), 90°)Fig. 6.3.90.25
Regular 90° elbow (2-in, screwed)Table 6.50.95
55%-open gate valveFig. 6.3.32.7
Sharp exitFig. 6.3.61.0
\(\sum K\)12.3

Note the bend here has \(R/d = 6\) (not the 12 of the chart’s illustrative example) because \(R = 12\) in but \(d = 2\) in — giving \(K \approx 0.25\), not 0.4.

4

Major loss: Reynolds number and friction factor

\[ \mathrm{Re}_d = \frac{Vd}{\nu} = \frac{(9.17)\left(\tfrac{2}{12}\right)}{0.000011} = 139{,}000 \quad\text{(turbulent)} \]

With \(\mathrm{Re}_d = 1.39\times10^5\) and \(\varepsilon/d = 0.001\), the Moody chart gives

\[ f = 0.0216 \]

5

Substitute into the pump-head equation

\[ h_p = 100\ \text{ft} + \frac{(9.17\ \text{ft/s})^2}{2(32.2\ \text{ft/s}^2)}\left[\frac{0.0216(400\ \text{ft})}{\tfrac{2}{12}\ \text{ft}} + 12.3\right] \]

\[ h_p = 100\ \text{ft} + (1.305\ \text{ft})\big[\,51.8 + 12.3\,\big] = 100\ \text{ft} + 83.7\ \text{ft} = 184\ \text{ft} \quad\text{(pump head)} \]

6

Convert pump head to power

\[ P = \rho g\,Q\,h_p = \big[1.94(32.2)\ \text{lbf/ft}^3\big](0.2\ \text{ft}^3/\text{s})(184\ \text{ft}) = 2300\ \text{ft}\!\cdot\!\text{lbf/s} \]

\[ P = 2300\ \text{ft}\!\cdot\!\text{lbf/s}\times\frac{1\ \text{hp}}{550\ \text{ft}\!\cdot\!\text{lbf/s}} = 4.2\ \text{hp} \]

Answer

Therefore the pump must deliver \(h_p \approx 184\) ft of head, requiring \(P \approx 4.2\) hp of power to the water. (The actual motor rating is higher, divided by the pump efficiency \(\eta_{\text{pump}}\).)
★ Tips & Traps

• Working in the BG system, specific weight \(\gamma = \rho g = 1.94(32.2) = 62.4\ \text{lbf/ft}^3\) for water — carry \(g\) explicitly so the slugs cancel into lbf.

• The sharp exit always contributes the full \(K = 1.0\); never drop it because “the pipe just ends.”

• Both \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) vanish only because the reservoir surfaces are the chosen points. If point 2 were the pipe exit, you would keep its velocity head.

• Single diameter throughout ⇒ one velocity head factors out; if the pipe changed size you would split the losses by segment.

Reference items used: Head equation (#43), Continuity \(V=Q/A\) (#18), Reynolds number (#47), Darcy–Weisbach (#48), Minor loss \(h_m=KV^2/2g\) (#57), Combined single-pipe loss (#59), Pump power (#45).

Key Takeaways

Chapter 6.3 in a Nutshell

• Minor losses are local, fitting-induced losses; “minor” means local, not small — they can dominate.

• Each is written as a multiple of velocity head: \(h_m = K\,V^2/2g\), with \(K\) supplied by experiment (charts/tables).

• The full system balance is \(h_{\text{loss}} = \sum h_f + \sum h_m\), fed into the head equation with \(+\)loss, \(-\)pump, \(+\)turbine.

• For a single diameter, factor out one velocity head: \(h_{\text{total}} = \frac{V^2}{2g}\!\left(\frac{f}{d}\Sigma L + \Sigma K\right)\). Multiple sizes ⇒ segment by segment.

• Standard values to keep close: sharp entrance \(K\approx0.5\), sharp exit \(K=1.0\); area-change losses use the smaller-pipe velocity head.
